articles.title: Go "method must have no type parameters": causes and fixes
articles.excerpt: Originally published on ImportStatic. Since Go 1.27, a method on a concrete type may declare its own type parameters. On a current setup, "method must have no type parameters" therefore means one of t…
articles.body: Originally published on ImportStatic . Since Go 1.27, a method on a concrete type may declare its own type parameters. On a current setup, "method must have no type parameters" therefore means one of two things: an older toolchain or an older go line in go.mod is still in charge, or the method is in an interface, where type parameters remain forbidden. The exact wording of the message tells you which. We compiled this file, a small slice type with a generic Map method, under Go 1.25.13, 1.26.10 and 1.27.3 and collected every message: type List [ T any ] [] T // Map has its own type parameter R: a generic method.

articles.title: Sentinel: The Rules Engine
articles.excerpt: Watchdog & Derived Points turned staleness and derived values into ordinary transitions on ordinary points, and The Command Plane took commands away from rules altogether. That leaves the rules engine…
articles.body: Watchdog & Derived Points turned staleness and derived values into ordinary transitions on ordinary points, and The Command Plane took commands away from rules altogether. That leaves the rules engine very little to do. A rule watches a few points, evaluates a condition when one of them changes, and holds a claim while the condition is true. A rule keeps no state between evaluations. It sees the current value and quality of each input, without timestamps or history, and a rule that needs a fifteen-minute average or a debounce takes a derived point as an input instead. So every rule is a pure function of what it reads. A restart can't leave a latch out of step with the world, and a test is a snapshot of inputs and the claims expected from it. A rule has two kinds of output.
articles.author: Philip Shaw

articles.title: Alpha Vantage limits and the Japanese stock gap
articles.excerpt: When I first went to wire up a stock data feed, Alpha Vantage looked like the obvious default: it's free, it's a real API, and it covers a huge swath of assets. So I wrote my pipeline against it — and…
articles.body: When I first went to wire up a stock data feed, Alpha Vantage looked like the obvious default: it's free, it's a real API, and it covers a huge swath of assets. So I wrote my pipeline against it — and then discovered two things that changed how I think about any free financial data feed. First, the free tier is rate-limited so tightly (I measured roughly 5 requests per minute) that any loop needs a sleep between calls. Second, and bigger for me: it doesn't cover Japanese stocks at all, which is the market I actually needed. Checked and confirmed in my own setup. The free tier is a scheduling constraint, not a firehose The headline "free" hides a real operational constraint. On the free tier I observed roughly 5 requests per minute, which is fine if your job makes a handful of calls.

The original is at https://mdodeja.github.io/eu-ai-act-article-50-guide/guides/booking-chatbot-ai-disclosure.html . Short answer. A booking chatbot needs the Article 50 disclosure like any other chatbot. When it takes a paid booking, the Consumer Rights Directive also applies, and Article 8(2) says the consumer must explicitly acknowledge the obligation to pay, with a button or similar function labelled "order with obligation to pay" or something equally clear. If that step is missing, the consumer is not bound.

articles.body: NASA is reviving discussions to rescue the Hubble Space Telescope, which is operating well but is on track to reenter Earth's atmosphere about six years from now. The agency issued a request for information (RFI) on Oct. 29 for "in-space servicing" capabilities, which could include boosting Hubble's orbit (which is naturally degrading due to atmospheric drag), or even a mission to "enhance its capabilities" in some way. articles.title: Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes
articles.excerpt: Collisions between stars in the early universe were common, and this could explain the growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Tele…
articles.body: New research suggests that collisions between stars in the early universe were common, which could help explain the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The team behind this research performed simulations of the early universe and found stellar systems were densely packed, leading to stars frequently slamming into each other. While rapid collisions would have destroyed the stars involved, slower collisions would have led to repeated mergers, creating single over-massive stars, which could collapse and form larger-than-usual black holes at the end of their lives. These could be the seeds of the first supermassive black holes.

articles.title: Dimorphos in sight: Europe's Hera probe gets its 1st look at battered space rock (photo)
articles.excerpt: Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart.
articles.body: Europe's Hera planetary defense spacecraft is closing in on the binary asteroid system targeted by NASA's DART deflection test, and can now tell the two rocky bodies apart. Hera is nearing the end of its voyage to the Didymos asteroid system, having launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in October 2024. The spacecraft snapped the image of Didymos and the smaller Dimorphos on Oct. 18 from a distance of 795 miles (1280 kilometers) from the pair, which are currently about 122 million miles (197 million km) from Earth. "With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," Michael Kueppers, Hera project scientist at the European Space Agency (ESA), said in a statement .

articles.title: Hubble Telescope sees cosmic 'cat's tail' that could wrap around Earth and the sun 500 times
articles.excerpt: Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail formed when two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together.
articles.body: Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail, finding it likely formed after two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together. The feature, nicknamed the Cat's Tail, extends out from the debris disk known as Beta Pictoris which is located in a planetary system located 63 light-years away. This tail would put that of the average tabby to shame: It's so long that it could curl around the sun-Earth system about 500 times. That's about as long as 200 trillion house cats. The major difference between our solar system and the planetary system that hosts the Cat's Tail is the latter's relative youth. While our solar system is around 4.6 billion years old , Beta Pictoris is a cosmic kitten no more than a few million years old.
